articles.body: DP World has appointed Jason Varsamidis as Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director of its Asia Pacific region, effective immediately. Varsamidis will lead DP World’s Asia Pacific portfolio of ports, terminals and logistics businesses across 22 geographies with more than 12,000 employees. Varsamidis brings close to three decades of experience with DP World and its predecessor P&O Ports, which he joined in 1997. He most recently served as Chief Financial Officer of DP World Asia Pacific since 2020, playing a central role in shaping the region’s strategy, investment agenda and business performance, and previously served as CFO of DP World Australia for seven years. Across his career he has overseen mergers and acquisitions, infrastructure projects and business turnaround programmes. In his new role, Varsamidis will focus on driving regional strategy and operational performance, strengthening end-to-end supply chains and expanding DP World’s integrated logistics capabilities across Asia Pacific. Group CEO Yuvraj Narayan described Varsamidis as a highly respected leader with deep understanding of the business and the markets in which it operates, noting that his track record and commercial acumen make him well placed to lead Asia Pacific as one of DP World’s key growth engines. Varsamidis expressed commitment to maintaining momentum, delivering for customers and partners and advancing strategic priorities across the region.

Bulgarian Interior Ministry/Handout via REUTERS BUCHAREST, Oct 17 (Reuters) – Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the country’s territorial waters on Saturday, the defense ministry said. The drones were brought down days after two chemical tankers were hit by drones near Romania’s Black Sea coast, the latest in a series of attacks highlighting risks to commercial shipping on NATO’s eastern flank. Both vessels were anchored near the Sulina Canal , which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is an export route for Ukraine. NATO member Romania shares a 614-km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, and has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Romania started shooting down such drones earlier this year. The defense ministry said the two drones entered Romanian waters in the Black Sea on Saturday at 1459 GMT and 1501 GMT, respectively. The ministry did not specify the origin of the drones. The two tankers struck earlier this week were hit by Russian drones, a NATO military source told Reuters. Romanian officials are still searching for seven missing crew members . At least five other cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of Romania and neighboring Bulgaria in the past 10 days, with 23 sailors reported dead or missing. Most of those incidents occurred outside NATO territorial waters. In Moldova, on Romania’s northeast border, officials said a new drone had crashed in a northern district, near the border with Ukraine. Officials said there were no casualties or damage and specialists were trying to determine the drone’s origin. The number of drones violating Moldovan airspace has increased greatly in recent months. Five drones identified as Russian fell on Moldovan territory in a little more than 17 hours on Thursday and Friday, prompting the foreign ministry to issue a statement denouncing Russian actions. articles.title: DP World deploys electric yard tractors at Busan
articles.summary: DP World has deployed 55 electric yard tractors at its Busan terminal in South Korea, replacing LNG-powered vehicles and accounting for approximately 36 percent of the terminal’s 154-strong yard tractor fleet. The new electric tractors are expected to reduce CO2 emissions by approximately 70% per unit compared to the...
articles.body: DP World has deployed 55 electric yard tractors at its Busan terminal in South Korea, replacing LNG-powered vehicles and accounting for approximately 36 percent of the terminal’s 154-strong yard tractor fleet. The new electric tractors are expected to reduce CO2 emissions by approximately 70% per unit compared to the LNG-powered machines they replace, representing a significant step in reducing emissions from terminal operations at one of Asia’s busiest container ports. As a participant in South Korea’s Emissions Trading Scheme, DP World Busan’s electrification programme aligns with both the company’s global decarbonisation commitments and South Korea’s broader ambitions for low-carbon logistics and greener port operations. Beyond emission reductions, the transition will reduce the use and disposal of engine fluids, minimising leak risks and the environmental impact of terminal operations. The electric tractors also offer quieter operation, smoother acceleration and more consistent performance during frequent stop-and-go movements, and with fewer moving parts than LNG-powered equivalents are expected to require less maintenance, supporting equipment availability and operational efficiency. Anders Dømmestrup, Chief Operating Officer for Ports and Terminals Asia Pacific at DP World, described the deployment as an important milestone demonstrating that progress on emissions reduction can be achieved while continuing to deliver safe, efficient and reliable customer services. The Busan deployment builds on similar electrification initiatives across DP World’s global terminal network, including the Port of Brisbane in Australia, Manila South Harbour in the Philippines and Laem Chabang International Terminal in Thailand. DP World Busan plans to continue expanding electric equipment adoption as part of its longer-term terminal emissions reduction strategy.

articles.title: Port of Montreal and Adani Group renew collaboration agreement
articles.summary: The Montreal Port Authority and the Adani Group have renewed their collaboration agreement during Team Canada’s trade mission to India, signed in Mumbai by Captain Sandeep Mehta representing the Adani Group and Marie-Claude Galarneau, Executive Vice-President and Chief Operating and Transformation Officer of the MPA,...
articles.body: The Montreal Port Authority and the Adani Group have renewed their collaboration agreement during Team Canada’s trade mission to India, signed in Mumbai by Captain Sandeep Mehta representing the Adani Group and Marie-Claude Galarneau, Executive Vice-President and Chief Operating and Transformation Officer of the MPA, in the presence of Canadian Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu. The renewal builds on a partnership that began with the first collaboration agreement in 2018. India has become one of the Port of Montreal’s most significant trading partners, ranking second among the port’s markets in 2025 with 1 million tonnes of goods exchanged, comprising 60 percent exports and 40% imports. Principal commodities include food products, ceramic products and plastics on the import side, and forestry and metal products on the export side. The renewed agreement focuses on developing trade through the Mundra-Montreal maritime corridor, joint promotion and information sharing to identify new business opportunities, sharing port and technological expertise to improve operations and road and rail transportation fluidity, and exploring new areas of collaboration including vehicle transportation. As part of its strengthened commitment to the Indian market, the MPA has appointed Prakash Tulsiani as its new agent in India, facilitating engagement with shipping lines, freight forwarders and importing and exporting companies and raising awareness of business development opportunities between the two countries. The initiative supports trade diversification and supply chain resilience against the backdrop of a changing global trade environment, with India projected by the IMF to become the world’s fourth-largest economy by 2027 to 2028. MPA President and CEO Paul Bird described India as a major trading partner and expressed ambition to facilitate trade and strengthen Montreal’s role as a strategic gateway between India and the economic heart of North America. Minister Sidhu highlighted the opportunity for Canadian businesses to reach one of the world’s fastest-growing economies, noting progress toward a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement with India.

articles.body: Xeneta: Carriers Accelerate Red Sea Return With Offered Capacity Doubling In Six Weeks in International Shipping News 17/10/2026 The Xeneta Weekly Ocean Container Shipping Market Update provides data and intelligence including the latest freight rate and capacity movements across global trades with supporting insight from Emily Stausbøll, Xeneta Senior Shipping Analyst. Xeneta analyst insight – Carriers accelerate Red Sea return with offered capacity doubling in six weeks Emily Stausbøll, Xeneta Senior Shipping Analyst: “The return of container shipping to the Red Sea is accelerating with offered capacity on services transiting or set to start transiting the region in at least one direction doubling in the last six weeks. “On 5 October, weekly scheduled capacity crossing Bab el-Mandeb at the gateway to the Red Sea in at least one direction stood at 448,273 TEU. While this is still only 48% of the 930,679 TEU offered in August 2023 before ships began diverting around Cape of Good Hope, the fact it has doubled since 27 August 2026 indicates a major shift in strategy from carriers. “Only carriers can answer what has changed in security assessments in the last six weeks to underpin such a dramatic acceleration in the return to the Red Sea, but whatever the reason, this will see capacity released back into the global fleet and have a profound impact on freight rates and services heading into 2027. “October does make sense in many ways for a ramping up in Red Sea rerouting because volumes typically come down following peak season. The capacity released into the fleet will also be partially absorbed by the current congestion in global ocean networks, at least for now. “Shippers must view this latest development in Red Sea services with the highest importance because it will be one of the drivers for ocean container shipping markets in 2027.” Carriers blank sailings to hold Far East to US rates as Far East to Europe finds its level “Spot rates from the Far East to the US have remained almost flat for the past month, but we are now in mid-October and through Golden Week, so downward pressure is expected to intensify. “The telling signal is that carriers are removing capacity, with 58,200 TEU blanked on the Far East to US West Coast trade this week and 35,500 TEU from Far East to US East Coast. “When spot rates on US trades are still up triple-digit percentages compared to pre-Hormuz crisis in February, carriers would normally be adding capacity rather than blanking sailings, so this looks like the behavior of carriers who don’t believe the market will hold and are protecting the current level rather than expecting further growth. “On the other side of the coin, Far East to Europe spot rates have stabilized following steady decline, even edging up 2.5% into North Europe and 3.2% into Mediterranean from a week ago. This is likely the balance of supply and demand correcting spot rates that have fallen far enough. “The Europe and US trades are telling a similar story at different price levels. Spot rates into the US East Coast are more than three times those into North Europe, but carriers cannot sustain a spread this wide for long. When the spread narrows it will be driven by rates into the US falling and to a much smaller degree Europe strengthening – that is exactly what we are now starting to see.” Data highlights Market average spot rates – 16 October 2026: Far East to US West Coast: USD 8,296 per FEU (40ft container) Far East to US East Coast: USD 11,495 per FEU Far East to North Europe: USD 3,568 per FEU Far East to Mediterranean: USD 4,165 per FEU North Europe to US East Coast: USD 2,946 per FEU Change from a week ago (since 9 Oct 2026): Far East to US West Coast: -0.2% Far East to US East Coast: -0.1% Far East to North Europe: +2.5% Far East to Mediterranean: +3.2% North Europe to US East Coast: +0.8% Red Sea return – scheduled weekly capacity crossing Bab el-Mandeb: Weekly offered capacity Aug 2023: 930,679 TEU Weekly offered capacity scheduled 5 Oct 2026: 448,273 TEU Source: Xeneta 2026-10-17 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Tanker Market Moved Higher in September in Hellenic Shipping News 17/10/2026 D irty tanker spot freight rates surged in September across all vessel classes, as trade dislocations, export inefficiencies and longer voyages kept tanker availability constrained, OPEC said in its latest monthly report. VLCC rates were close to doubling on all monitored routes, except on the West Africa-to-East route where rates were closer to tripling. On the Middle East-to-East route, VLCC spot freight rates were up 88%, m-o-m, in September, while rates on the West Africa-to-East route increased 142%, m-o-m. Suezmax spot freight rates benefited from a spillover in demand from the VLCC sector. On the USGC-toEurope route, Suezmax rates increased 53%, m-o-m. Aframax rates also joined the upward trend in September. On the Intra-Med route, Aframax spot freight rates gained 87%, m-o-m. In the clean tanker market, spot freight rates showed considerable strength in the East of Suez, where rates increased 54% on average, m-o-m, while West of Suez spot rates increased by 13%. Dirty tanker freight rates Very large crude carriers (VLCC) VLCC spot freight rates registered new record highs in September, as trade dislocations, export inefficiencies, and increased tonne-mile demand limited tanker availability. On average, VLCC spot freight rates increased 98%, m-o-m, and were up 981%, or roughly eight times higher, y-o-y. On the Middle East-to-East route, spot freight rates averaged WS962 in September. This represents a m-o-m increase of 88% and a gain of 981%, or almost eleven times higher, than in the same month last year. On the Middle East-to-West route, spot freight rates averaged WS440. This represents an increase of 87%, m-o-m, while y-o-y rates were up 730%, or more than eight times higher. Rates on the West Africa-to-East route saw the biggest jump in September, with a 142% gain over the previous month to reach WS421. Compared to the previous year, rates were up 390%, or almost five times higher. Suezmax Exceptional strength in VLCC rates encouraged charterers to look to the Suezmax market, boosting rates. On average, Suez spot freight rates increased 53%, m-o-m. Compared with the same month last year, Suezmax rates were 246%, or over three times higher. On the West Africa-to-USGC route, spot freight rates averaged WS373 in September, representing an increase of 53%, m-o-m. Compared with year-ago levels, rates were 259% higher. Rates on the USGC-to-Europe route averaged WS313, also reflecting a 53% increase over the previous month. Y-o-y, rates were 233% higher. Aframax Aframax spot freight rates saw gains on all monitored routes in September, m-o-m, as the proverbial rising tide lifted all boats. On average, rates increased 72%, m-o-m. Compared with the same month in 2025, Aframax rates were up 19%, or about four times higher. Spot freight rates on the Indonesia-to-East route increased by 62%, m-o-m, to average WS307. Y-o-y, rates on the route were up 144%. Rates on the Caribbean-to-US East Coast (USEC) route registered the weakest increase, gaining 25%, m-o-m, to average W416. Compared with the same month last year, rates were up 170%. Meanwhile, rates around the Mediterranean saw the strongest gains on monitored Aframax routes. Cross-Med rates increased 87%, m-o-m, to average WS452 in September. Rates on the Med-to-Northwest Europe (NWE) route increased 73%, m-o-m, to average WS411. Compared with the same month in 2025, rates were 232% and 214% higher, respectively. Clean tanker freight rates In the clean tanker market, East of Suez increases outpaced those in the west. In September, East of Suez spot freight rates increased 54%, m-o-m, on average, and were up 277%, or about four times higher, y-o-y. West of Suez spot rates increased 13%, m-o-m, while West of Suez rates were up 32%, y-o-y. Rates on the Middle East-to-East route were assessed at WS792, representing a gain of 45%, m-o-m. Compared with September 2025, rates were up 439%. Clean spot freight rates on the Singapore-to-East route increased 76%, m-o-m, to average WS392. Y-o-y, rates on the route were up 133%. Rates on the NWE-to-USEC route increased 16%, m-o-m, to average WS132. This represents a 16% gain from the same month last year. Rates on the Cross-Med and Med-to-NWE routes were up 12% each, m-o-m, to average WS209 and WS219, respectively. Y-o-y, spot freight rates on both routes were up 42% and 39%, respectively. articles.title: What lessons can we learn from declining carrier schedule adherence and rising port congestion?
articles.summary: Schedule reliability has fallen to near record lows in recent months, while port congestion has built up. In this opinion piece, Drewry experts draw the main lessons from the operational problems of the 2026 peak season to inform concerned shippers, forwarders, carriers and ports. Look at it from the viewpoint of a...
articles.body: What lessons can we learn from declining carrier schedule adherence and rising port congestion? in International Shipping News 17/10/2026 S chedule reliability has fallen to near record lows in recent months, while port congestion has built up. In this opinion piece, Drewry experts draw the main lessons from the operational problems of the 2026 peak season to inform concerned shippers, forwarders, carriers and ports. Look at it from the viewpoint of a shipper moving goods by containership on the Asia-Europe route. The proportion of ships on this route which arrived on the scheduled day of arrival declined from 51% in May to just 31% in September (average of all ports and all carriers), according to the Drewry Container Capacity Insight. Even the Gemini alliance, which has a higher-than-average track record for on-time arrivals, managed just 34% in September. All the ocean carriers under-perform on schedule adherence on this route. Shippers and forwarders are increasingly aware that, not only are the ships arriving late, but also a proportion of the intended sailings do not happen (so-called “blank sailings”). If we combine the 2 types of unpredicted changes and delays, then the proportion of performed and on-time sailings on the Asia-Europe route falls to about 29% in September. Not all carriers and alliances are the same. The Asia-Europe trade’s schedule reliability scores by carrier in September ranged between 19% and 38% and the proportion of sailings not cancelled ranged between 0% and 23%, according to Drewry’s analysis for this route. Informed and realistic shippers and forwarders, therefore, must conclude that the best they can do is to monitor and compare their providers’ shaky schedule adherence, switch to those who are above-average when possible… and build “buffer time” in their supply chains. This is because the cargo will, more often than not, arrive later than promised by the carrier at the time of booking. Peak season buffer time may need to be longer, too. If ocean carriers are under-performing on schedule adherence, they can still say that many ports and terminals, particularly in Asia, have been gridlocked during the summer, making it impossible to meet scheduled arrivals and departures for their ships. The data below shows the reverse relationship between schedule reliability for ships arriving at the port of Shanghai and berthing waiting times at the port of Shanghai. The picture is fairly clear: when berth congestion in the port of Shanghai rose from about 1.6 to 3.9 days, Shanghai reliability collapsed from 55% to 10%. The all-ports figure on schedule reliability for all Asia-Europe ships also followed it down. By contrast, there is no close statistical correlation between berth congestion at the port of Rotterdam, Europe’s largest container port, and Asia-Europe schedule reliability for ships arriving at the port Rotterdam. The lesson then is that it is critical to watch and monitor port congestion at the big Asian ports – as this influences schedule reliability on many routes. Another lesson is the somewhat counter-intuitive link between the worsening of port congestion in Shanghai during the peak season and the increase in the proportion of Asia-Europe sailings not cancelled. Looking at this from a carrier viewpoint, the logic is that cargo volumes were strong in the peak season, port congestion got worse in Asia, but the carriers could make higher profits by throwing more ship capacity at the market and cancelling fewer sailings… which must have made port congestion worse. Another conclusion, Drewry believes, is that recent months have shown that timely operations by ports and by ocean carriers did not rank at the top of their priorities. (See Drewry’s recent opinion piece on this here www.drewry.co.uk/news/port-congestion-is-getting-worse-in-container-shipping-who-is-responsible ) Our view: Schedule reliability and port congestion are likely to remain significant challenges for the industry, and there is little to suggest that these pressures will disappear anytime soon. For shippers, the question is what they can do differently. Simply allowing more time is one option, but it doesn’t necessarily address where the risks sit within their supply chains. At Drewry, we are looking more closely at how carrier performance, port congestion and network exposure can be brought together to give shippers a clearer picture of where they may be vulnerable. It is not about predicting every disruption, but about understanding the risks and making better-informed decisions. Ultimately, the aim should be to move away from simply reacting to delays and towards building those risks into carrier selection, procurement strategies and contingency planning. After all, knowing that a vessel is likely to be late is useful. Understanding what that delay means for your supply chain, and what you can do about it, is far more valuable. Note Unlike other market intelligence providers, who calculate schedule reliability by comparing actual times of arrival (ATA) and estimated times of arrival (ATA) published around 15 days before the arrival, the Drewry Container Capacity Insight online tool follows a more demanding methodology which aims to compare ATA vs ETA published close to the time of booking. Therefore Drewry collects ETAs between 2 weeks and 6 weeks before vessel arrival. Source: Drewry Tops 2026-10-17 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: in International Shipping News 17/10/2026 S chedule reliability has fallen to near record lows in recent months, while port congestion has built up.
In this opinion piece, Drewry experts draw the main lessons from the operational problems of the 2026 peak season to inform concerned shippers, forwarders, carriers and ports.
Look at it from the viewpoint of a shipper moving goods by containership on the Asia-Europe route.

articles.title: Security doesn’t stop time bars
articles.summary: The English Court of Appeal’s recent decision in Batavia Eximp & Contracting (S) Pte Ltd v Pedregal Maritime SA [2026] EWCA Civ 1158 provides an important reminder of the distinction between obtaining security for a maritime claim and preserving the underlying claim itself. The Court held that proceedings brought...
articles.body: Security doesn’t stop time bars in International Shipping News , Shipping Law News 17/10/2026 T he English Court of Appeal’s recent decision in Batavia Eximp & Contracting (S) Pte Ltd v Pedregal Maritime SA [2026] EWCA Civ 1158 provides an important reminder of the distinction between obtaining security for a maritime claim and preserving the underlying claim itself. The Court held that proceedings brought purely to obtain security do not constitute “suit” for the purposes of the one-year time bar in Article III rule 6 of the Hague-Visby Rules. The decision also provides useful guidance on what a bill of lading must say where only part of a cargo is to be carried on deck and therefore potentially excluded from the Hague-Visby regime. Pedregal Maritime SA owned the Taikoo Brilliance and issued four bills of lading for the carriage of a cargo of New Zealand pine logs to Kandla, India. Batavia Eximp & Contracting (S) Pte Ltd held the bills. The cargo was discharged in September 2019 without production of the original bills of lading and against a letter of indemnity provided by the vessel’s charterer. The holders alleged that the cargo had been misdelivered. The bills provided for London arbitration. However, in August 2020, and within the one-year Hague-Visby time bar, the holders commenced proceedings in Singapore and arrested the Navios Koyo, a sister ship of the Taikoo Brilliance. Security was provided and the vessel was released. The owner successfully obtained a stay of the Singapore proceedings in favour of London arbitration. The Holders only commenced the arbitration in December 2020, more than one year after delivery of the cargo. The arbitrator held that the Singapore proceedings did not prevent the Article III rule 6 time bar from applying. That conclusion was upheld by the Commercial Court and has now been confirmed by the Court of Appeal. Obtaining security is not the same as bringing the claim Article III rule 6 provides that the carrier and ship are discharged from liability in respect of the goods unless “suit is brought” within one year of delivery or the date when the goods should have been delivered. The question was whether the Singapore arrest proceedings were sufficient to constitute “suit”, notwithstanding that the substantive dispute was required to be determined in London arbitration. The Court of Appeal held that they were not. In context, “suit” means proceedings which seek to establish the carrier’s substantive liability. Proceedings brought merely to obtain security for a claim do not satisfy that requirement where they are not capable of determining the underlying liability. The Court considered that this interpretation was consistent with the purpose of the Article III rule 6 time bar. The rule is intended not only to ensure that carriers receive prompt notice of claims, but also that those claims are promptly pursued and that there is commercial finality. If proceedings for security alone were sufficient, a claimant could arrest a vessel within the one-year period and potentially leave the substantive claim to be commenced much later. That would undermine the certainty which the time bar is intended to achieve. The practical result is straightforward: obtaining security does not, by itself, preserve the underlying Hague-Visby claim. The substantive proceedings must still be commenced in time in a forum competent to determine the claim. Which cargo is actually on deck? The Court of Appeal also considered a separate issue concerning the part of the cargo carried on deck. Article I(c) excludes from the definition of “goods” cargo which is stated in the contract of carriage to be carried on deck and is in fact carried on deck. Such cargo therefore falls outside the Hague-Visby regime. Two of the bills recorded the total number of logs shipped and the number carried on deck at the shipper’s risk. They did not, however, identify which particular logs were carried there. That mattered because the individual pieces of timber varied significantly in weight and therefore in value. The Court held that, where only part of a consignment consisting of items of differing value is carried on deck, the bill must specifically identify the cargo to be carried there, for example by parcel or serial number. Merely stating the number of items carried on deck was insufficient. The reason is practical. Cargo carried on deck and cargo carried below deck may be subject to different liability regimes and different risks. The shipper and subsequent holders of the bill must therefore be able to determine, from the contractual documentation, which cargo falls into which category and manage their risks accordingly. The Court left open precisely what would be required where the cargo is homogeneous or its constituent items do not differ in value. Key learnings The most useful aspect of Taikoo Brilliance is perhaps the distinction it draws between securing a maritime claim and preserving it. Vessel arrests are frequently used to obtain security for claims which will ultimately be determined elsewhere, whether by a foreign court or in arbitration. The judgment makes clear that obtaining that security should not be confused with taking the procedural steps necessary to preserve the underlying claim. Cargo interests and their insurers should therefore consider the two issues separately. An arrest may result in perfectly adequate security being put in place, but the applicable contractual and statutory time bars must still be considered and the substantive proceedings commenced in the appropriate forum within time. The deck-cargo issue carries an equally practical lesson for carriers. Where only part of a consignment is to be carried on deck, the bill of lading should identify that cargo as clearly as possible. This is particularly important where the individual items differ in value, since the designation may determine whether the Hague-Visby Rules apply and may also affect the risks which cargo interests need to insure. The judgment ultimately emphasises the importance of certainty at both stages. Obtaining security does not preserve a claim which has not been pursued in time, and a general reference to deck cargo may not be sufficient to determine which goods fall outside the Hague-Visby regime. Source: Baltic Exchange, Clyde & Co. Tops 2026-10-17 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: The Court held that proceedings brought purely to obtain security do not constitute “suit” for the purposes of the one-year time bar in Article III rule 6 of the Hague-Visby Rules.
The decision also provides useful guidance on what a bill of lading must say where only part of a cargo is to be carried on deck and therefore potentially excluded from the Hague-Visby regime.
Pedregal Maritime SA owned the Taikoo Brilliance and issued four bills of lading for the carriage of a cargo of New Zealand pine logs to Kandla, India.

articles.title: Container carriers adjust rates, add services to Americas, continue gradual return to Suez
articles.summary: Global container shipping companies are increasing rates along some trade lanes, adding stops to existing services to the Americas, and improving transit times between India and the US East Coast via gradual returns to the Suez Canal. PRICE HIKES Global container shipper CMA CGM will raise rates for shipments between...
articles.body: Container carriers adjust rates, add services to Americas, continue gradual return to Suez in International Shipping News 17/10/2026 Global container shipping companies are increasing rates along some trade lanes, adding stops to existing services to the Americas, and improving transit times between India and the US East Coast via gradual returns to the Suez Canal. PRICE HIKES Global container shipper CMA CGM will raise rates for shipments between Oceania and the Americas by $300/TEU (20-foot equivalent unit) effective 2 November. The increase is for cargo moving in both directions, including from Oceania to both North and South America, as well as shipments from the east coasts of the US and Canada and the US Gulf to Oceania. The adjustments cover dry containers, refrigerated cargo, out-of-gauge (OOG) shipments and paying empty containers. CMA CGM is also increasing rates from Asia to South America by $1,000/container effective 15 October. This covers cargoes originating in all Asian ports, including Japan, Southeast Asia and Bangladesh. The increase applies to dry, reefer and out-of-gauge cargo, as well as paying empty containers. Maersk is introducing a peak season surcharge (PSS) on dry container shipments from the East Coast of South America to the US and Canada effective 5 November. The PSS will be $1,000/container for both 20-foot and 40-foot containers. Maersk is also increasing its import/export fuel surcharge for US inland cargo beginning 1 November to $215/container from $140/container because of rising US fuel prices. The charge will apply to cargoes carried under a Maersk ocean bill of lading where the carrier arranges trucking to or from the customer’s door within the US. NEW STOP IN SUAPE Global container shippers Mediterranean Shipping Co (MSC) and Maersk are adding Suape, Brazil, to their shared service between the US Gulf and Mexico to the East Coast of South America. The MSC Yamuna VI will make the first Suape call on 26 October. Reasons for the adjustment include seasonal export demand, peak Asia-EC South America volumes and broader resiliency in strategies to deal with volatile global supply chains. RETURN TO SUEZ CUTS INDIA-SAVANNAH TRANSIT TIME Shipments from India are now reaching the US East Coast port of Savannah 10 to 14 days faster as carriers slowly begin returning to the Suez Canal route. The Georgia Port Authority (GPA) said the shift back through the Suez Canal of Maersk’s MECL service, the INDAMEX service from CMA CGM and announcements from MSC to restore some services will shorten the time to move goods between India and the US East Coast. “Georgia Ports welcomes the transit time improvements as several major carriers return to Suez routings linking Georgia to world markets,” Kevin Price, President of Georgia Ports, said. It has been almost three years since commercial shipping lines began avoiding the Red Sea/Suez Canal trade lane, a much shorter route for trade between Europe and Asia, because of attacks on vessels in the Red Sea from Iran-backed Houthis. The longer route around the Cape of Good Hope initially strained capacity and sent container freight rates soaring. Container ships and costs for shipping containers are relevant to the chemical industry because while most chemicals are liquids and are shipped in tankers, container ships transport polymers, such as polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP), which are shipped in pellets. Titanium dioxide (TiO2) is also shipped in containers. They also transport liquid chemicals in isotanks. articles.title: GMS Week 42 – Freight Finally Flinches
articles.summary: The dry freight retreat gathered pace this week, bringing awaited relief for recycling buyers without yet producing the ships they need. The Baltic Dry Index recorded a steep weekly fall, led by Capesizes, while recycling indications across all four destinations remained unchanged. Owners now face a less comfortable...
articles.body: GMS Week 42 – Freight Finally Flinches in Weekly Demolition Reports 17/10/2026 The dry freight retreat gathered pace this week, bringing awaited relief for recycling buyers without yet producing the ships they need. The Baltic Dry Index recorded a steep weekly fall, led by Capesizes, while recycling indications across all four destinations remained unchanged. Owners now face a less comfortable outlook for larger bulkers, but one week’s correction cannot overturn months of profitable trading. Freight has blinked. The sellers have not. The Strait of Hormuz supplied a troubling counterweight. Singapore-registered GFS Pride was struck on October 13 and subsequently sank after catching fire; GFS Giselle sustained hull damage in a separate incident the next day. All 43 crew members were reported safe. The attacks sharpened concerns over passage, security and insurance, keeping disruption in voyage calculations. For ageing tankers, altered routes and restricted effective availability can still make further employment more attractive than recycling. Oil markets also absorbed an intervention. On October 15, the International Energy Agency announced plans to accelerate release of approximately 100 million barrels remaining under its March emergency stock programme, following around 330 million barrels already released. Brent nevertheless remained around USD 105 to 106 per barrel on Friday. Additional inventories may ease supply pressure, but cannot remove Gulf shipping risks. The cost of disruption survives the arrival of extra barrels. Dry bulk was the more immediate source of encouragement for recyclers. The Baltic Dry Index fell from 2,973 on October 8 to 2,545 on Thursday, October 15, a decline of more than 14%. Capesizes dropped from 4,512 to 3,322, while Panamaxes eased to 2,356. Supramaxes moved against the trend, improving to 1,856. The uneven retreat matters: larger bulkers may be feeling pressure, but smaller and mid-sized ships continue to find worthwhile employment. Falling indices alone do not deliver vessels to the beaches. Steel supplied no common regional signal. Bangladesh plate rose from BDT 64,000 to BDT 66,000 per ton despite subdued finished-steel demand. Indian plate finished at INR 42,300, below last Friday, although the stronger Rupee lifted its Dollar equivalent to USD 445.17. Pakistan eased to PKR 195,000, while Turkey faced weak domestic steel consumption and currency pressure. India’s September inflation rose to 5.54%, complicating financing and demand. None of this altered the recycling price board. Physical activity still exceeded fresh business. Alang delivered the 31,300 LDT LNG carrier Kano on October 15, reinforcing India’s specialist position. Chattogram added several bulker and tanker arrivals, and Gadani delivered two previously secured bulkers. These movements represent ships already in the pipeline, not newly agreed sales. Bangladesh retains the conventional pricing lead, Pakistan remains competitive, India concentrates on specialist value, and Turkey holds its established regional position. No fresh market sales were reported this week. The next test is whether dry freight declines for long enough to change owners’ decisions. The correction is real, but tanker employment remains supported by Gulf disruption, while smaller dry sectors have surrendered little ground. Recycling buyers have maintained their numbers without securing a fresh supply of candidates. The market has started moving in their direction, although it has not arrived there yet. Owners will need more than one uncomfortable week before the beaches see the benefit. For Week 42 of 2026, GMS Market Rankings / Vessel indications are as below. articles.body: The Week in Alt Fuels: Building the bunker menu in International Shipping News 17/10/2026 Bunkering activity came in many flavours this week, with biofuels, LNG, LBM, methanol, ethanol and ammonia featuring across several major ports – and sometimes with multiple fuels at the same port. China’s Ningbo-Zhoushan port offered perhaps the clearest illustration of this variety. On 30 September, three bunker vessels supplied LNG, methanol and B24 biofuel to different ships at three terminals on the same day. It was the first time three different marine fuels had been supplied on the same day at the port, according to the Ningbo Maritime Safety Administration. The names of the receiving vessels and fuel suppliers were not disclosed. The volumes were substantial. Around 3,300 mt of LNG, 7,500 mt of methanol and 3,000 mt of B24 were delivered across the port. Ammonia bunkering also took place in China in the past week. Belgian shipping company CMB.TECH’s first ammonia-capable bulk carrier, Mineral Europa, was bunkered with 1,000 mt of green ammonia in a ship-to-ship (STS) transfer at Zhoushan. The operation was carried out by the ammonia bunker vesselShenghang Yongle. Singapore also had a busy week on the alternative fuels front. Bunker supplier Golden Island is set to deliver bio-ethanol at Pasir Panjang Terminal in an operation involving shipping company Maersk and terminal operator PSA Singapore. French shipping company CMA CGM partnered with the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) and Singapore LNG (SLNG) to explore LBM bunkering. The agreement follows Shell’s recent import of mass-balanced LBM into Singapore and the arrival of its chartered LNG bunker vessel Macoma at the SLNG terminal. The MPA also introduced new technical guidelines for ammonia bunkering at the port, covering custody transfer, bunkering procedures, safety measures and crew training. Vitol Bunkers is preparing to enter the physical LNG bunker supply market in Singapore and other Asian ports later this year, following sea trials of its 12,500-cbm bunker vessel Vivit Asia LNG. The LNG activity has not been confined to Singapore. The LNG-capable car carrier AICC Fenghuang recently received around 2,600 cbm of LNG at the Port of Hong Kong before sailing for the Mediterranean. The STS transfer was carried out by CLPe and CNOOC (Shenzhen) International Marine Clean Energy. In Spain, Axpo completed its first LNG bunker delivery in Valencia, with LBM accounting for more than half of the fuel supplied. Beyond the physical deliveries, bunker infrastructure was also in focus. CMA CGM and energy company ENGIE are planning a biomethane production plant at Haropa Port in Le Havre, France. The facility is expected to produce around 7,000 mt/year of biomethane from 2029, with CMA CGM planning to take the entire output for its LNG dual-fuel fleet. CMB.TECH is developing an ammonia bunker terminal at Walvis Bay in Namibia. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2027, with completion expected in late 2028 or early 2029. Investors in bunker infrastructure face “location-specific” commercial risks, CMB.TECH’s chief technology officer Roy Campe told ENGINE. Unlike dual-fuel vessels, which can continue running on conventional fuels while the ammonia market develops, a terminal depends on sufficient demand at a particular port. CMB.TECH expects its own fleet to provide initial demand at Walvis Bay, but third-party customers will be needed to support the terminal’s commercial viability. In other news this week, logistics firm DSV will use CMA CGM’s biofuel bunkering service to claim around 12,000 mtCO2e of well-to-wake emissions reductions for its ocean freight operations. The Biofuel Company of Saudi Arabia (TBFCO) plans to work with local bunker suppliers in Qatar to arrange physical deliveries of 100% biofuel (B100) to vessels at Qatari ports, a company spokesperson told ENGINE. Swedish shipping company Wallenius Marine will explore how ships can be better designed to harness wind power, rather than retrofitting conventionally designed vessels with wind-assisted propulsion systems. The research project will run from 2026 to 2029 and examine how a vessel’s shape and deck layout influence the performance of wing sails and other wind propulsion technologies. Source: By Konica Bhatt, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news/ 2026-10-17 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: China’s Ningbo-Zhoushan port offered perhaps the clearest illustration of this variety.
On 30 September, three bunker vessels supplied LNG, methanol and B24 biofuel to different ships at three terminals on the same day.
It was the first time three different marine fuels had been supplied on the same day at the port, according to the Ningbo Maritime Safety Administration.

articles.summary: French shipowner LD Armateurs has completed the installation of six towering rotor sails aboard Spirit of Toulouse, a new roll-on/roll-off vessel being built to transport aircraft components for Airbus across...

Join the leading maritime news network Caption: LD Armateurs’ Spirit of Toulouse, built for Airbus transatlantic transport operations, fitted with six 35-meter-tall Norsepower rotor sails at an outfitting site in Shanghai, China. Photo: LD Armateurs/Norsepower French shipowner LD Armateurs has completed the installation of six towering rotor sails aboard Spirit of Toulouse , a new roll-on/roll-off vessel being built to transport aircraft components for Airbus across the Atlantic. The installation, completed at a shipyard outfitting site in Shanghai, makes the 168-meter vessel the largest RoRo ship equipped with wind-assisted propulsion and gives it more mechanical sails than any other ship, according to LD Armateurs and Finnish wind propulsion specialist Norsepower. Each of the six rotor sails stands 35 meters tall and measures 5 meters in diameter. The rotating cylinders harness wind to generate additional thrust, reducing the workload on the ship’s main engines and, in turn, its fuel consumption. The vessel is also equipped with two dual-fuel main engines and two generator sets capable of operating on e-methanol, bio-methanol or marine diesel oil. The combination is intended to reduce fuel consumption and emissions without relying entirely on alternative fuels. Spirit of Toulouse is the first of three sister ships being built for LD Armateurs under charter to Airbus. The other two vessels, Spirit of Mobile and Spirit of Mirabel , will also receive six rotor sails each. The ships will transport large aircraft assemblies between Airbus production facilities in Europe and North America, replacing the manufacturer’s existing transatlantic fleet. Airbus expects the new fleet to cut annual emissions from its transatlantic shipping operations by more than half, from approximately 68,000 metric tons of CO2 in 2023 to 33,000 metric tons by 2030. Those reductions will depend on a combination of improved vessel efficiency, wind propulsion and the availability of lower-emission fuels. “Completing installation of six Norsepower Rotor Sails on Spirit of Toulouse is a significant milestone for wind propulsion in the RoRo segment,” said Heikki Pöntynen, CEO of Norsepower. The vessel was launched in February and is preparing for sea trials, during which the rotor sails will undergo testing. Further adjustments are planned during its maiden voyage from China to France. Wind Propulsion Gains Ground The project comes as wind-assisted propulsion moves beyond individual demonstration projects and finds wider use across the commercial shipping fleet. According to the International Windship Association (IWSA) , more than 100 large commercial vessels were equipped with wind propulsion systems as of June 2026, carrying more than 230 individual installations. That compares with just 21 large vessels in May 2022, representing nearly a fivefold increase in four years. Tankers and bulk carriers have led the expansion, although RoRo ships, ferries and general cargo vessels are increasingly adopting the technology. Earlier this year, Berge Bulk completed the installation of four folding rotor sails on its 208,000-dwt Newcastlemax bulk carrier Berge Meru , following a similar project aboard the larger Berge Neblina in 2024. In August, the Ultramax bulk carrier Maria Topic returned to commercial service after receiving a rigid wingsail during a retrofit at Tsuneishi Shipbuilding in Japan. And in September, Spanish shipowner Marflet Marine installed four 22-meter suction sails aboard the 49,999-dwt chemical tanker Santiago I , with technology supplier bound4blue estimating the system could reduce annual energy consumption by approximately 10% to 15%. The growing range of installations reflects the different approaches being used to capture wind energy. Rotor sails use spinning cylinders to generate thrust through the Magnus effect, while other systems employ rigid wings, suction sails or even kites. Unlike conventional sailing vessels, most wind-assisted merchant ships continue to rely on their main engines for propulsion, using wind power to reduce fuel consumption whenever conditions allow. The technology has also produced measurable results. In an earlier trial involving the Maersk Pelican product tanker, two Norsepower rotor sails delivered an independently validated 8.2% reduction in fuel consumption over one year. More recently, Cargill reported that the bulk carrier Pyxis Ocean , fitted with two large WindWings, achieved average fuel savings of approximately three metric tons per day during a six-month trial. With two more Airbus vessels to follow, the project will provide another test of how those technologies perform together in regular commercial service. articles.title: Fog of War Deepens in Hormuz as UKMTO Says Most Ship Attacks Go Unreported
articles.summary: Conflicting traffic figures and competing claims of control are making it increasingly difficult to establish what’s happening in the Strait of Hormuz, even as attacks on merchant shipping intensify. The...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, September 28, 2026. Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/via WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS Conflicting traffic figures and competing claims of control are making it increasingly difficult to establish what’s happening in the Strait of Hormuz, even as attacks on merchant shipping intensify. The true extent of attacks on merchant ships in the Strait of Hormuz remains unclear, with a new report from UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) acknowledging that most vessels struck in the region are not reporting incidents directly to the maritime security organization. The admission comes as the United States and Iran offer sharply different accounts of who controls the vital waterway, while conflicting transit figures raise further questions about how much commercial shipping has actually recovered. In its weekly overview published Friday , UKMTO said it is struggling to establish the true number of attacks because the majority of vessels targeted are refusing to submit reports. UKMTO said it is aware of additional incidents through other sources but cannot include them in its reporting without sufficient verification. The disclosure raises questions about the reliability of publicly available attack statistics, particularly following a sharp escalation in strikes against commercial vessels over the past two weeks. UKMTO recorded 12 attacks during its latest reporting period, including 10 in the Strait of Hormuz, one in the Arabian Gulf and one in the Gulf of Oman. Six vessels continued their voyages or reached port, two were disabled or left not under command, and three had unconfirmed damage or outcomes. One vessel, the Singapore-flagged containership GFS Pride , was lost after being struck by a projectile. The report also found that 55 of 74 documented projectile strikes since July 6 occurred along the southern route through the strait, accounting for nearly three-quarters of the reported attacks. The findings stand in contrast to increasingly confident statements from U.S. military officials about their control of the waterway. In a video statement Friday, Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, said American forces and regional partners remain firmly in control of the strait despite continued Iranian attacks. “Let me be clear: the Strait of Hormuz is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran. And it remains open for business,” Cooper said. He reported that approximately 400 merchant ships had transited the strait over the preceding seven days, while U.S. forces helped Gulf partners move more than 100 million barrels of crude oil during the same period. Cooper said those shipments added to more than 1.3 billion barrels of crude transported with U.S. assistance in recent months. But the latest UKMTO figures paint a different picture. For the seven days ending October 14, UKMTO recorded 254 combined transits, including 129 inbound and 125 outbound movements. That was down from 275 the previous week, with traffic remaining approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels. Of those 254 movements, just 42 were observed through Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. The remaining 212 were drawn from U.S.-reported facilitated transits, which include ships operating without broadcasting AIS. UKMTO cautioned that the U.S.-supplied figures and associated totals cannot currently be independently verified. Cooper did not specify the exact dates covered by his 400-transit figure, leaving open the possibility that the difference reflects separate reporting periods or counting methods. Nevertheless, the gap illustrates the difficulty of establishing a consistent picture of commercial traffic through the strait. Iran, meanwhile, continues to dispute Washington’s account of control over the waterway. Iranian army chief Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami said Thursday that the strait would remain closed until the rights of the Iranian people were respected. The latest Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) advisory , published October 15, describes both a northern Iranian-controlled route and a southern Omani corridor, while warning that ships operating with AIS switched on face an elevated risk of targeting and instructions to divert toward the Iranian route. UKMTO’s latest report adds that most vessels broadcasting AIS continue to use the Iranian route, even as U.S.-facilitated traffic accounts for the majority of reported transits. The competing accounts reflect the increasingly complicated security environment for merchant shipping. U.S. forces are facilitating substantial traffic through the strait, while Iran continues to demonstrate an ability to strike vessels, including those using the southern corridor. And with UKMTO now acknowledging that most attacked vessels are not reporting incidents directly, even the growing number of documented strikes may offer only a partial picture of the dangers facing seafarers. articles.title: Fincantieri Integrates AI, Robotics to Advance Shipyards
articles.summary: Fincantieri is accelerating the transformation of its shipyards through the integration of advanced robotics, Physical AI, and next-generation automation systems, with the aim of making production processes increasingly efficient, safe, and…
articles.body: Fincantieri Integrates AI, Robotics to Advance Shipyards Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 Credit: Fincantieri Fincantieri is accelerating the transformation of its shipyards through the integration of advanced robotics, Physical AI, and next-generation automation systems, with the aim of making production processes increasingly efficient, safe, and competitive. This is the vision behind BOOST² – The Shipyard of the Future, the industrial innovation program launched by the Group three years ago to identify, develop, and integrate new technologies into its production processes. Throughout its journey, the initiative has engaged more than 450 Fincantieri employees across 13 shipyards in Italy and abroad, including facilities in Romania and the United States, fostering direct interaction with operational needs and actively involving people in the development of new solutions. As part of the Industrial Plan, the program provides for investments of almost 100 million euros. The program’s latest achievements were presented at the Castellammare di Stabia shipyard through demonstrations of solutions already in operation, technologies currently undergoing validation, and applications destined for further evolution. Following an initial phase focused on technology scouting and experimentation, the program is now geared towards accelerating the transition from innovation to industrial deployment, supporting the adoption of new solutions in day-to-day operations and their progressive rollout across the Group’s shipyards. This approach builds on the results achieved so far and aims to further strengthen the integration of technologies, industrial expertise, and the practical needs of production. In this context, collaboration with the innovation ecosystem plays a key role. Through its Open Innovation strategy, Fincantieri identifies and selects technology partners in Italy and internationally, including SMEs and start-ups, to develop and tailor solutions to the specific needs of the shipbuilding industry. The direct involvement of people and production teams is an integral part of the process, enabling field testing, accelerating adoption, and ensuring that technologies can be scaled and replicated across different manufacturing environments. At the heart of the program are Physical AI, which enables intelligent systems to interact with the physical world, and collaborative robotics, with applications designed to support people in carrying out the most complex tasks. These technologies are complemented by Digital Twin solutions for the digital management of shipyard assets and processes, Smart Supply Chain systems, additive manufacturing, and automated solutions for industrial equipment. The objective is to unlock the full potential of these technologies by progressively integrating them into operational workflows and strengthening the connection between design, planning, and production.

Stock Photo: Nickeo23/Shutterstock Deal adds four modern crude tankers as International Seaways reports sharply higher spot earnings entering the fourth quarter. International Seaways has agreed to acquire Oslo-listed Bruton Limited in a deal valued at approximately $370 million, adding four very large crude carriers (VLCCs) to its fleet as tanker earnings remain elevated. The New York-based tanker owner announced the agreement Friday, saying the acquisition will expand its fleet of approximately 70 crude oil and product tankers. The deal includes one VLCC already in operation and three newbuildings under construction at China’s New Times Shipyard. The acquisition comes alongside preliminary financial results showing strong tanker market conditions. International Seaways reported average blended spot earnings of approximately $68,000 per day during the third quarter, more than double the $29,000 per day recorded a year earlier. Rates have climbed further entering the fourth quarter. The company said it has secured blended spot earnings averaging approximately $180,000 per day for about 37% of its expected fourth-quarter revenue days. Under the acquisition agreement, International Seaways will initially acquire a 50.5% stake in Bruton through a share exchange with existing shareholders, expected to settle around October 20. The company will then acquire the remaining shares through a cash-and-stock merger. International Seaways expects to issue approximately 3.12 million shares as part of the transaction, accounting for roughly 96% of the total consideration. The remainder will be paid in cash. Bruton shareholders are scheduled to vote on the merger around October 30, with the transaction expected to close shortly afterward, subject to customary conditions. “We’re excited about the opportunity to expand and modernize our fleet through this accretive transaction with Bruton,” said Lois K. Zabrocky, president and CEO of International Seaways. “The transaction underscores our disciplined approach to growth.” Bruton’s fleet consists of the 300,000-dwt Mount Vision, delivered in July, and three sister vessels scheduled for delivery between November 2026 and October 2027. According to Bruton’s fleet information, Mount Vision is earning $95,000 per day under its existing charter, while the next vessel, Mount Horizon, has secured a charter at $105,700 per day. Bruton previously controlled a larger VLCC newbuilding program, but spun off eight vessels into OMC Tankers, which began trading in Oslo in August. Those eight newbuildings are not part of the International Seaways acquisition. International Seaways also expects third-quarter revenue of $480 million to $490 million and net income of $340 million to $350 million, including an approximately $50 million gain from the sale of a 2012-built Suezmax tanker. The company reported liquidity of approximately $965 million at September 30, including $455 million in cash and short-term investments. Its full third-quarter financial results are scheduled for release on November 5. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Port of Long Beach The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach both set all-time monthly cargo records in September, handling a combined 2.04 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) as strong imports and shifting global trade patterns continued to drive cargo through the nation’s busiest port complex. The Port of Long Beach reported Thursday that it handled 997,177 TEUs in September, up 25% from a year earlier and surpassing its previous record of 987,191 TEUs set in October 2024. It was the busiest month in the port’s 115-year history. The milestone follows last week’s record-breaking announcement from the Port of Los Angeles , which handled 1,042,652 TEUs in September, the highest monthly total in its 118-year history. Together, the neighboring ports moved 2,039,829 TEUs in September, including more than 1.05 million TEUs of loaded imports, as retailers continued replenishing inventories and shippers adjusted their routing strategies amid high fuel costs, trade uncertainty and disruptions along other major shipping routes. “Shippers continue to lean on the Port of Long Beach as a reliable partner in their business strategies, leading to our historic month for cargo,” said Port of Long Beach CEO Noel Hacegaba during the port’s monthly Supply Chain Insight briefing. Imports led the surge at Long Beach, climbing 31.3% from a year earlier to 509,390 TEUs. Exports increased 7.8% to 91,747 TEUs, while empty container movements rose 22.1% to 396,040 TEUs. Los Angeles reported similarly strong numbers, with loaded imports rising 19% to 545,696 TEUs. The port also handled 125,751 TEUs of exports and approximately 371,206 empty TEUs, both increases from a year earlier. Port officials have attributed the strong performance to several factors, including resilient consumer demand, lower U.S. tariffs and shippers seeking alternatives to traditional routes affected by Panama Canal restrictions and security concerns around the Suez Canal. High diesel prices have also made the shorter transpacific route to the U.S. West Coast more attractive. The record-breaking September comes as the National Retail Federation (NRF) expects the unusually long peak shipping season to finally wind down. In its latest Global Port Tracker report , released October 8, NRF and Hackett Associates projected that imports at major U.S. container ports would ease from 2.3 million TEUs in August to 2.28 million TEUs in September, followed by 2.25 million TEUs in October and 2 million TEUs in November. “Even with any fluctuations in final data, we’re likely past the busiest part of the year,” said Jonathan Gold, NRF vice president for supply chain and customs policy. The forecast follows months of stronger-than-expected imports that extended the traditional peak season well into the fall. Notably, both Southern California ports have reported handling the increased volumes without the congestion that disrupted operations during the pandemic. At Long Beach, Total Terminals International set a new monthly rail record in September, handling 59,410 rail moves, representing nearly half of the terminal’s container volume. Long Beach has now handled 7,675,255 TEUs through the first nine months of 2026, up 3.9% from the same period last year. Los Angeles has processed nearly 8.1 million TEUs over the same period, more than 3% ahead of last year’s pace. articles.title: Houthi Attacks on Saudi Arabia Defy Difference in Military Power
articles.summary: The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are demonstrating the limits of the kingdom’s military prowess — despite defense spending that far outstrips that of its regional neighbors.

REUTERS/Khaled Abdullah By Gerry Doyle (Bloomberg) — The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are demonstrating the limits of the kingdom’s military prowess — despite defense spending that far outstrips that of its regional neighbors. Missiles and drones fired by the Iran-backed group from Yemen have wreaked havoc in Saudi Arabia in recent days, killing at least 18 people and forcing the closure of the country’s main international airport in Riyadh. The Houthis are showing no sign of scaling back their campaign, targeting several Saudi Arabian cities in an assault this week that’s continued into Thursday. Saudi Arabia allocated between $64 billion and $96 billion this year for defense, according to data compiled by Bloomberg Economics. The upper end is more than twice as much as Israel, the next biggest Middle East spender. The kingdom operates Raytheon Co. Patriot missile batteries with the latest Lockheed Martin Corp. PAC-3 interceptors, flies hundreds of Boeing Co. F-15 fighters customized for its air force, and is the only Gulf country with mid-air refueling aircraft. One reason the Houthis have been able to cause such destruction with less advanced equipment is Saudi Arabia’s size, which complicates defense efforts. The kingdom covers more than 2.1 million square kilometers (830,000 square miles), with many strategic targets to protect, from oil infrastructure to air bases to several large cities. Defending against ballistic missiles is complex when protecting a single target, let alone sites sprinkled across a vast country. Thousands of Iranian strikes across the Arabian peninsula during the initial phase of the US and Israeli war on the Islamic Republic were largely thwarted by missile defenses, but even a 90% success rate can mean massive damage on the ground. Saudi Arabia’s military is also still in the process of modernizing and remains heavily reliant on the US for military intelligence. The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment. The most recent rounds of Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have tended to involve a mix of weapons that further complicate defensive efforts: small drones, low-flying, cheap cruise missiles and ballistic missiles. In addition, the Houthis are a nimble, rapidly evolving opponent backed by Iran, capable of building and deploying missiles and drones that can challenge even advanced defense systems. Years of fighting in Yemen mean the group is battle hardened, resisting protracted military efforts to dislodge or contain them. “The Houthis are partly beneficiaries of good fortune, but they seem remarkably adaptive,” said Ankit Panda, Stanton Senior Fellow in the Nuclear Policy Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “A determined attacker armed with missiles is still difficult to deal with.” The Houthi arsenal has now evolved to the point where the group can manufacture relatively precise drones and ballistic missiles — some of which rely on parts from Chinese companies. Those munitions might cost thousands, or hundreds of thousands of dollars, far cheaper than the multimillion-dollar air defense interceptors used to stop them. That means even a successfully intercepted attack imposes further costs on Saudi Arabia, and makes it more vulnerable to future strikes. Defensive weapons such as the Iranian-made 358 surface-to-air missiles — which can loiter at high altitudes and strike subsonic aircraft — make the skies over Yemen dangerous too. Another issue, said Bloomberg Economics defense lead Becca Wasser, is that Patriot air defense batteries are directional. They do not cover a 360-degree area, so if radars and launchers were positioned to intercept Iranian fire, they may not have been able to easily shoot down Houthi missiles, she said. Air and missile capabilities have improved as part of Saudi Arabia’s modernization efforts, Wasser said. Although pilots learned considerably from the long Yemen air war, their aircraft remain largely reliant on the US for targeting data, in particular. The situation has improved since Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman began a reform agenda, alongside “real-life experience in its first war against Yemen,” Wasser said. “But modernization is slow and confined to pockets of bright spots rather than upskilling across the force.” Although Riyadh has a fleet of more than 200 F-15 jets — almost as many as the US Air Force — it was unable to use them decisively in more than a decade of bombing the Houthis. Saudi Arabia went to war with the militant group in 2015 after it took control of the Yemeni capital, Saana, though fighting receded between a 2022 truce and the recent flare up. “Equipment and funding do not win wars,” said Wolf-Christian Paes, a senior fellow for armed conflict at the International Institute for Strategic Studies. “Training, motivation and leadership do.” US influence in the Middle East after 1990 — when Washington intervened after Iraq invaded Kuwait — prompted many countries in the region to rely on US firepower rather than fully develop their own capabilities. Saudi Arabia was not immune to this “protection curse,” said David Roberts, a reader in international security and Middle East studies at King’s College London. US struggles in Afghanistan, and incidents like the 2019 Houthi drone attack against oil facilities in Abqaiq, in the east of Saudi Arabia, punctured the image that “Uncle Sam would basically detect and protect,” Roberts said. US President Donald Trump has so far opted against intervening directly in the current conflict. In a post on Truth Social on Tuesday he said the Houthis were “behaving very badly,” without specifying what action the US could take. Saudi Oil Minister Prince Abdul Aziz Bin Salman said this week that “the events of recent weeks are serious,” adding that the kingdom’s response “must be equally serious, while remaining focused on the decades ahead.” The Houthis began threatening shipping in the Red Sea after the start of the war in Gaza, which prompted the US to briefly intervene, launching more than 1,000 strikes over three months. But hunting down hidden, mobile launchers and shutting down buried production facilities is difficult, especially in the rugged terrain in which the Houthis operate. The operation ended with a ceasefire. The Houthis show “there are very clear limits what an air campaign can do,” said April Longley Alley, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. Former US Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin, speaking at the Warsaw Defense Forum on Monday, said Saudi Arabia would most likely need help from friendly nations to counter the Houthi threat. “There will be a concerted effort to get the Houthi thing under control,” he said. “But it won’t be easy. They are much more resilient than most people recognize.” The conflicts in Iran and Ukraine have shown how the power of ballistic missiles, particularly those with a range of 1,000 kilometers or more, mean even countries whose millitaries are relatively weak can cause problems for more powerful adversaries. The Houthis’ strike arsenal includes indigenously produced Quds-1 cruise missiles, which have a reach of about 750 kilometers, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Its homegrown ballistic arsenal is larger, with Burkan-1, -2, and -3 designs, which can fly 600 kilometers, 850 kilometers and 1,200 kilometers, respectively, giving the militants the range to hit nearly any site in Saudi Arabia. Riyadh’s struggles to extinguish the Houthi threat and defend against counterattacks reflects the difficulty of a task many others have failed at too. “Yemen is a hard nut to crack. The US couldn’t do it,” Longley Alley said. “This is something that can’t be solved with a military tool only.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche LONDON, Oct 16 (Reuters) – The cost ?of shipping oil on the largest tankers fell this week from record highs as demand eased following a wave of attacks on vessels in the Middle East and as the US considered easing sanctions on the so-called shadow fleet. Freight rates ?for supertankers, also known as very large crude carriers (VLCCs), carrying oil ?from the Gulf of Oman to China fell to about 776 ?on the Worldscale basis, according to Baltic Exchange ?data. That was down from 841 last week, the highest since the rate was launched earlier this year, following gains since the outbreak of the Iran war. “Gulf of Oman VLCC rates dropped as demand on that route has softened since the fresh attacks, as higher Middle East Gulf freight rates and subsequently lower export volumes have reduced demand on this route,” said Kpler analyst Matthew Wright. Trump administration comments about potentially removing sanctions on some shadow-fleet tankers drove freight rates lower, Sparta Commodities analyst Michael Ryan said, adding a removal would increase the number of ships that can carry oil. Despite the drop, rates remain close to record highs. The US-Israeli war on Iran has increased the use of ship-to-ship transfers to move oil out of the Strait of Hormuz, boosting demand for tankers. If elevated shipping costs persist, they could add to inflationary pressures and raise costs for businesses and consumers. Rates have also eased from record highs on other routes this week, such as from West Africa to Asia. (Reporting by Enes Tunagur in London. articles.summary: Three senior House Republicans are calling on the Department of Homeland Security to revoke special inspection privileges granted to vessels operated by Chinese state-owned shipping giant COSCO, citing allegations that...

File Photo: Port of Long Beach Three senior House Republicans are calling on the Department of Homeland Security to revoke special inspection privileges granted to vessels operated by Chinese state-owned shipping giant COSCO, citing allegations that the company’s ships have been used to collect intelligence near U.S. coastlines. In an October 14 letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, House Intelligence Committee Chairman Rick Crawford and Rep. Carlos Gimenez, chairman of the Homeland Security Subcommittee on Transportation and Maritime Security, called for COSCO vessels to be removed from the U.S. Coast Guard’s Qualship 21 program. The program rewards foreign-flagged vessels with strong safety and compliance records by allowing them to undergo fewer routine port state control inspections at U.S. ports. According to the lawmakers, at least 10 COSCO vessels were enrolled in the program as of July 15, despite the company’s designation by the Pentagon as a Chinese military company. An accompanying Coast Guard table identifies 11 vessels, including COSCO DEVELOPMENT , COSCO PRIDE and COSCO VIETNAM . The letter, which has now prompted a Coast Guard review, follows a September 1 Reuters investigation in which two senior Trump administration officials alleged that COSCO uses concealed equipment aboard its commercial ships to intercept military communications near the coastlines of the United States and other countries. The officials said the alleged intelligence-gathering operations were part of a decades-long relationship between COSCO and Beijing, allowing China to collect communications signals from ships and aircraft operating across Europe, North America and Asia. COSCO denied the allegations in a September statement, saying its onboard equipment serves legitimate commercial purposes, including navigation, communications and emergency response, and is not used for intelligence gathering or military surveillance. China’s embassy in Washington also rejected the allegations. The lawmakers argue that the reported activities warrant a review of whether COSCO should continue receiving preferential treatment under the Coast Guard program. “State-owned commercial vessels engaging in espionage is an expected breach of trust we regularly anticipate from the Chinese Communist Party,” the lawmakers wrote. They called on DHS to revoke COSCO vessels’ enrollment, refuse renewals and increase scrutiny of other companies suspected of conducting activities on behalf of China’s People’s Liberation Army. Beyond removing COSCO from Qualship 21, the lawmakers are seeking answers about what the Coast Guard knew about the alleged surveillance activities and when that information became available. They specifically asked whether Coast Guard Intelligence received warnings about COSCO from the Pentagon, intelligence agencies or other federal authorities before the September 1 Reuters report, and whether that information was considered when determining the vessels’ eligibility. In a statement to gCaptain, a Coast Guard spokesperson confirmed that on October 15, the Commandant has directed an immediate review of the vessels’ participation. “The U.S. Coast Guard is responsible for the safety and security of U.S. ports, waterways, and shipping, which are vital to our nation’s economic prosperity and national security. Every day, the Coast Guard takes decisive action to identify, mitigate, and address safety and security risks to our ports in the physical domain and cyberspace.” The lawmakers also questioned whether COSCO’s designation under Section 1260H, which identifies Chinese military companies operating in the United States, prompted a review of the company’s Qualship 21 status. Other questions concern whether the Coast Guard has conducted additional boardings of COSCO ships, whether it has sufficient authority to investigate suspected surveillance activities in U.S. waters, and whether analysts are examining historical vessel movements in the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone for patterns that could indicate intelligence collection. The letter also calls for a review of Hong Kong’s continued eligibility as a qualified flag administration under Qualship 21, citing concerns about Beijing’s control over the territory. The Coast Guard updated its Qualship 21 eligibility criteria earlier this year, expanding the circumstances under which vessels can be removed from the program, including certain associations with sanctioned entities and companies facing federal criminal investigations. “The U.S. Coast Guard continuously evaluates and updates its programs to address the dynamic and evolving security and safety landscape of the maritime industry,” the Coast Guard told gCaptain. “ The congressional request raises a separate question of whether national security intelligence and military-company designations should factor into decisions about which foreign vessels qualify for reduced inspections. Qualship 21 enrollment does not exempt vessels from security inspections or other Coast Guard enforcement actions, and the lawmakers’ request does not itself revoke COSCO’s eligibility. The Department of Homeland Security has not publicly announced any action in response to the letter.
