articles.title: All American Marine Build Report: October 2026
articles.summary: All American Marine recently launched M/V North Star, the second high-speed, long-range eco-tour vessel built for Phillips Cruises & Tours. Like her sistership, Chugach Express, North Star will operate from Whittier, Alaska, carrying passengers…
articles.body: All American Marine Build Report: October 2026 Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Ron Wille, President, All American Marine October 16, 2026 Credit: AAM All American Marine recently launched M/V North Star, the second high-speed, long-range eco-tour vessel built for Phillips Cruises & Tours. Like her sistership, Chugach Express, North Star will operate from Whittier, Alaska, carrying passengers through the tidewater glaciers and wildlife-filled waters of Prince William Sound. The 84.5-foot, hydrofoil-assisted aluminum catamaran features a Teknicraft Design semi-displacement hull and is certified to USCG Subchapter T standards for up to 150 passengers. Her propulsion package mirrors that of Chugach Express: four MJP 350X waterjets driven by quad 800 mhp Scania DI16 082M engines, paired with Teknicraft’s dynamic hydrofoil system and wave-piercing bow. A repeat order is performance data in its clearest form. After operating Chugach Express through three demanding Alaska seasons, with full passenger loads, long days, and changing conditions. Phillips knew this platform could deliver. One of the most notable changes is fuel capacity with Chugach Express carrying 1,200 gallons, while North Star carries 1,600. The increase did not require a redesign; it was made possible by proven performance. Chugach Express demonstrated that the hull could carry additional weight without sacrificing speed, efficiency, or ride quality. The second vessel uses that margin to add 400 gallons and extend its operating range. But range is only part of the story. The Teknicraft hull and dynamic hydrofoil system are designed to reduce vessel accelerations underway, while the hull form and foil provide added motion damping at rest. For passengers, that means a more comfortable ride. For operators, it means a broader usable weather window, supporting more operating days, greater schedule reliability, and stronger revenue potential. That capability matters in Prince William Sound. Maintaining comfortable speeds in changing sea conditions can preserve more time at the destination while keeping the return schedule within reach. It can also mean the difference between completing a tour and remaining at the dock. Last month, we examined how little fuel consumption changes between light and fully loaded conditions on a Teknicraft hull. North Star shows what an operator can do with that margin. Greater fuel capacity, strong seakeeping, and efficient performance combine to create something more valuable than any single specification: greater operating capacity. WHAT OPERATORS ARE ASKING Top speed tells only part of the story. Passenger vessel operators need to know how a vessel rides at full load in real conditions, how guests feel after five or six hours aboard, and how much of the schedule can be maintained when the weather turns. Those are seakeeping questions, and on a tour vessel, they show up in two places. The first is underway. During transit, the Teknicraft hull form and hydrofoil lift work together to reduce vertical accelerations, the pounding and slamming that wear on passengers and crew over a long day. The second is on scene. At a glacier’s face or alongside a pod of humpbacks, low-speed motion is often when passengers begin to feel unwell. Here, the hull form and foil help dampen that motion. Guests stay on deck, crews remain ready to work, and fewer people become what one of our operators calls “mal de mer zombies.” One additional advantage comes in the adjustable hydrofoil. By de-tuning it, captains can make the vessel ride “heavier” at wildlife-viewing speeds, settling the hull and creating a steadier viewing platform. The vessel remains light and fuel-efficient during transit, then becomes more planted once on scene. Weather is where seakeeping becomes operating capacity. These hulls can maintain comfortable speeds in conditions that force other vessels to slow down or remain at the dock. That broader operating window supports more completed trips, greater schedule reliability, and stronger revenue potential. WHAT IT SIGNALS As Alaska’s tour season winds down, passenger vessel operators head into the off-season with a full season of results in hand. That is when a vessel should be evaluated, by what it delivered through months of real service. What these operators have learned is straightforward: comfort is operating capacity. A vessel that can sail comfortably in more conditions completes more departures, issues fewer refunds, and protects revenue. A vessel that remains steady at low speed keeps guests on deck and engaged. A hull with additional carrying capacity gives operators options, and Phillips Cruises and Tours chose to turn that margin into greater range. Real performance is measured across the entire operating day: at full load, through a full season, and in the weather operators encounter, not the weather they started the season wishing for.

articles.body: Incat Crowther to Build Fourth Fast Support Intervention Vessel Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 Credit: Incat Crowther Zamil Offshore commissioned Incat Crowther and Singaporean shipbuilder Lita Ocean to design, build and deliver a fourth 60-m ABS-classed monohull Fast Support Intervention Vessel (FSIV). The project follows the delivery of the third vessel in the original fleet with the performance of the fleet leading to the order of a fourth vessel. The FSIV fleet is assisting Zamil Offshore with the efficient and safe transport of cargo, heavy maintenance equipment and personnel for Saudi Aramco’s operations in the Arabian Sea. Capable of speeds up to 36 knots, the vessels are powered by four MTU 16V4000 diesel engines coupled to ZF gearboxes driving Hamilton HT810 waterjets . Maneuverability of the DP2-certified vessels is enhanced by three Hydromaster tunnel bow thrusters , allowing safe docking and offshore station-keeping for transfer of cargo and personnel. Two of the main engines are coupled to FFS firefighting pumps paired with 1200 cu. m./hr. water monitors and shipboard water spray protection offering FiFi-1 capability. Three Scania 300kW diesel generators provide ship service power. The main deck offers an expansive 250 sq. m. aft cargo deck rated at 2.5 t/ m2 along with an optional Palfinger PK12000M deck crane . A climate-controlled forward cabin features business-class seating for 56 service personnel, as well as two bathrooms, a 15 sq. m. workshop, a 15 sq. m. storage room, a lounge and snack bar. Conducted ahead of Singapore’s 17th Joint Oil Spill Exercise (JOSE) 2026…
articles.body: Singapore Conducts Oil Spill Response Drill Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 Credit: Adobe Stock/Peter Hermes Furian Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia conducted a ground deployment exercise (GDX) under the Revolving Fund Committee to strengthen coordination in responding to oil spills in the Straits of Malacca and Singapore. Conducted ahead of Singapore’s 17th Joint Oil Spill Exercise (JOSE) 2026, the GDX simulated an oil spill originating from a vessel collision in Singapore waters, with the oil subsequently reaching the shores of Indonesia and Malaysia. Led by the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA), the GDX tested information sharing, response planning and mutual assistance among the three littoral States. As part of the exercise, Indonesia and Malaysia deployed response assets in their respective waters to test their response arrangements under the exercise scenario. Separately, MPA hosted representatives from government agencies, industry partners and international organisations at the Integrated Operations Hub (IOH) Lab at ALICE@Mediapolis as part of JOSE 2026. The program provided an opportunity to share Singapore’s oil spill response capabilities and explore how emerging technologies could support future response operations. Representatives from the International Maritime Organization (IMO), ITOPF[1], Indonesia’s Directorate General of Sea Transportation and Malaysia’s Department of Environment also attended the program. Participants were briefed on the coordinated deployment of response assets for oil containment, dispersal and recovery, drawing on demonstrations conducted at sea. The program also highlighted how emerging technologies could enhance oil spill response. These included MPA’s Maritime Digital Twin (MDT), which uses modelling to predict the movement of spilled oil and identify potentially affected areas, as well as artificial intelligence to support response planning and resource deployment. Participants were also briefed on potential concepts of operations involving unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned surface vessels (USVs), including those trialled with ST Engineering. Drawing on demonstrations conducted at sea, the briefing illustrated how aerial surveillance could guide USVs in carrying out tasks such as dispersant spraying and oil containment boom towing. Overall, JOSE explored how such concepts of operations could be supported as unmanned technologies mature, potentially expanding the range of capabilities available for future oil spill response operations.

articles.title: Estonia's First Electric Ferry Takes Shape in Poland
articles.summary: Steerprop was selected to supply its next-generation contra-rotating propeller (CRP) technology for Estonia's first fully electric passenger ferry, currently under construction at Poland's CRIST SA shipyard.The 95-meter ferry, designed by LMG Marin for the Estonian State Fleet…
articles.body: Estonia's First Electric Ferry Takes Shape in Poland Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 The 95-meter ferry, designed by LMG Marin for the Estonian State Fleet, will feature two Steerprop SP 25 CRP units equipped with permanent magnet motors. Image courtesy Steerprop Steerprop was selected to supply its next-generation contra-rotating propeller (CRP) technology for Estonia's first fully electric passenger ferry, currently under construction at Poland's CRIST SA shipyard. The 95-meter ferry, designed by LMG Marin for the Estonian State Fleet , will feature two Steerprop SP 25 CRP units equipped with permanent magnet motors. The propulsion system is designed to deliver high thrust and improved efficiency in both open water and ice conditions. Steerprop's CRP configuration uses two contra-rotating propellers on a single shaftline, allowing greater thrust and efficiency than comparable single-propeller arrangements. The latest generation introduces pressure lubrication, replacing immersion lubrication to reduce mechanical losses and improve mechanical efficiency by approximately 3.5 percentage points. "The latest Steerprop CRP development has resulted in a propulsor with unique efficiency and thrust performance, and one that offers an even greater performance boost for vessels operating in ice conditions," said Markku Miinala, Steerprop's Cruise & Ferry Segment Director. The ferry will incorporate a 3 MWh battery system charged using renewable shore power, supplemented by biodiesel generators for severe weather and emergency operations. Designed to 1B Ice Class requirements, the vessel will be capable of operating in ice up to 60 centimeters thick. Steerprop already supplies propulsion systems for four double-ended ferries operating on Estonia's Saaremaa and Hiiumaa routes. The propulsion equipment is scheduled for delivery in late 2027, with the ferry expected to enter service in late 2028. The vessel's design and construction contract is valued at €49.93 million, including €28 million in funding from the European Union Modernization Fund, with additional financing from Estonia's CO₂ quota trading mechanisms. Image courtesy Anglo Eastern Anglo-Eastern has detailed its role in developing and preparing CMB.TECH's Mineral Europa, the world's first ammonia-powered dry bulk carrier, which recently embarked on its maiden voyage. The 210,000 dwt Newcastlemax, built by CSSC Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding, features a WinGD dual-fuel ammonia engine and a Sun Rui Ammonia Fuel Supply System. The vessel can operate on ammonia or conventional marine fuel, providing flexibility as ammonia bunkering infrastructure develops. Anglo-Eastern's involvement dates to 2018, when its technical services division began evaluating alternative fuels with CMB.TECH, initially examining hydrogen before progressing to ammonia. By 2020, Anglo-Eastern Technical Services (AETS) was developing the vessel's safety philosophy, fuel arrangements and preliminary engineering. The design received Approvals in Principle from Lloyd's Register and ABS in 2021. A central engineering challenge was integrating ammonia storage, double-wall piping, ventilation, leak detection, containment and emergency shutdown systems without sacrificing cargo capacity. "The technical challenge was not just accommodating a new fuel. Safety, containment and operational requirements all had to work together as an integrated system without compromising the vessel's primary purpose as a commercial cargo carrier," said Arunava Sengupta, Managing Director of AETS. Anglo-Eastern also supported newbuilding supervision, technical management and crew preparation. Vessel-specific operating, bunkering, maintenance and emergency procedures were developed alongside training incorporating a three-dimensional digital twin, fuel supply simulator and emergency scenarios. Senior officers participated in shipyard and sea trials. "Mineral Europa demonstrates what can be achieved when an owner's conviction is matched by deep engineering and operational capability," said Bjorn Hojgaard, Anglo-Eastern CEO. CMB.TECH CEO Alexander Saverys described the vessel's entry into service as a milestone in the company's decarbonization strategy, with additional ammonia-powered vessels expected to follow. articles.title: Uncertain IMO Rules Weigh on Shipping’s Demand for Cleaner Marine Fuels
articles.summary: Shippers' appetite for lower-carbon marine fuels weakened this year as the fate of a regulatory emissions framework from the International Maritime Organization (IMO) remained cloudy while some are using carbon credits, industry executives said.IMO…
articles.body: Uncertain IMO Rules Weigh on Shipping’s Demand for Cleaner Marine Fuels Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 © Pawinee / Adobe Stock Shippers' appetite for lower-carbon marine fuels weakened this year as the fate of a regulatory emissions framework from the International Maritime Organization (IMO) remained cloudy while some are using carbon credits, industry executives said. IMO member nations are set to meet by early November on the formal adoption of a net-zero framework to guide the industry towards zero carbon emissions by 2050, after last year's vote to delay the move. Demand for marine biofuel, a more readily available alternative fuel on which shippers have focused more, has softened this year at the world's largest bunker hub of Singapore. Marine biofuel sales at the port totalled about 603,000 tons between January and September, down 47% from the corresponding 2025 period, government data showed. Total 2025 volumes had more than doubled from 2024. "I don't expect the biofuel demand to increase so much until we have an IMO decision," said Jens Maul Jorgensen, a director of dry bulk shipowner Oldendorff Carriers. "If anybody wants to have just a slightly greener world, IMO will have to step up," he told Reuters. "What we see now at the moment is a surplus of (carbon) credit to the FuelEU Maritime, and that is competing with biofuel (uptake)," added Jorgensen, speaking on the sidelines of the Singapore International Bunkering conference (SIBCON). He was referring to an EU regulation that requires ships exceeding gross tonnage of 5,000 tons and calling at EU ports to reduce emissions. While the FuelEU Maritime regulation has supported biofuels uptake in the European bunker hub of Rotterdam, the demand increase fell short of expectations. "Some of the tax benefits in Europe have prompted a little more uptake on biofuels, but in general we are a little bit surprised about the lack of demand," said Peter Grunwaldt, chief executive at Cargill-Hafnia joint venture Seascale Energy. "Even though biofuels (post-Iran war) are cheaper than gasoil (on some occasions), we are seeing people stick with gasoil. That's a little bit of a surprise to us, that the demand is not greater," said Grunwaldt. Total bio-blended bunker sales at Rotterdam have risen 28% in the year's first half over the first half of 2025, port data showed. "We need clear regulatory signals for the industry to work with," said Jesper Sorensen, global head of alternative fuels at KPI OceanConnect. "Right now, the only regulatory things in place are the emissions trading system and the FuelEU." The US-Israeli war with Iran has prompted more shippers to continue diversifying supplies, however. "Shipowners who have ordered alternative-fuel tonnage and dual-fuel tonnage are building optionality into their fuel mix," added Sorensen. "The disruption in the Middle East has shown that optionality is a good thing." Fossil-based marine fuel prices this week are at least 70% higher than levels before the Iran war began in February. (Reuters - Reporting by Jeslyn Lerh and Florence Tan; Editing by Clarence Fernandez)

articles.body: Environment Europe Operations Ports and Logistics Regulatory UK ports hit back at Brussels over ETS diversion claims Adis Ajdin October 16, 2026 0 1,365 3 minutes read UK Government UK Government British ports have challenged European Union claims that shipping lines are diverting container traffic to the UK to escape carbon charges, warning that proposed anti-evasion measures risk penalising billions of pounds of investment in British terminals. The British Ports Association (BPA) has rejected findings from Spain’s EU ETS Observatory linking rising UK container activity to the bloc’s Emissions Trading System, arguing that new capacity, changing liner networks and commercial competition offer more convincing explanations. In a new report, the association said around 85% of the UK’s container traffic growth in 2025 was concentrated in London, following the opening of DP World’s £350m ($465m) fourth berth at London Gateway in late 2024. Government figures show UK ports handled 11% more containers last year, equivalent to an additional 600,000 units. London accounted for roughly 500,000 of those, with its growth driven largely by the additional capacity at London Gateway. The DP World terminal handled more than 3m teu in 2025, up 52% from 1.9m teu a year earlier. The increase followed the opening of the fourth berth, which boosted capacity by more than a third, and the arrival of Asia-Europe services operated by Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd’s Gemini Cooperation in February 2025. London Gateway has been challenging Felixstowe’s position as Britain’s busiest boxport, with Maersk’s departure from the Hutchison-operated facility reshaping the country’s container market. DP World is pressing ahead with another £1bn ($1.33bn) expansion, adding two all-electric berths and a second rail terminal. The BPA argues that such investment and network changes have been overlooked in assessments linking Britain’s expanding container business to EU carbon pricing. The dispute follows research by Spain’s Puertos del Estado, which found the UK’s share of northern European deepsea shipping activity, measured in teu-miles, rose from 17.5% in 2023 to 32.1% by July 2025. Subsequent analysis put the figure at around 36% in the first quarter of 2026, broadly mirroring declines in Germany and the Netherlands. The Spanish study also estimated that 76% of observed route changes were attributable to the EU ETS, raising concerns that containerlines were restructuring their networks to reduce carbon costs. But the BPA has questioned both the methodology and the conclusions. It argues that teu-miles, which combine vessel capacity with voyage distance, measure shipping network activity rather than actual containers handled. The metric can also be distorted by longer voyages around the Cape of Good Hope and changes to the sequence of port calls. The association also disputes treating the widely cited 76% figure as evidence of carbon-driven diversion specifically to Britain, arguing that the available analysis does not isolate the effects of ETS from alliance restructuring, congestion and new terminal capacity. Continental European ports have not uniformly lost ground either. Rotterdam’s container throughput increased 3.1% to 14.2m teu in 2025, Hamburg recorded 7.3% growth to 8.3m teu, while Antwerp-Bruges posted a 0.7% increase. The disagreement comes after the European Commission proposed tightening rules designed to prevent containerships from using neighbouring non-EU ports to reduce their ETS exposure. Under proposals unveiled in July, certain container ports within 150 nautical miles of an EU port could be excluded from the definition of a port of call for emissions accounting purposes. The threshold for transhipment activity at other qualifying non-EU ports within 300 nautical miles would also be lowered from 65% to 50%. The changes could bring more British terminals within the EU’s anti-evasion framework, potentially increasing carbon costs for shipping lines using them. The proposals have yet to be adopted. “It would be extraordinary if the EU responded to that success by introducing new measures to penalise British ports,” said Mark Simmonds, the BPA’s director of policy and external affairs. The association stressed that it supports shipping decarbonisation but warned against treating normal competition between ports as regulatory avoidance. Britain has already brought domestic shipping and emissions in UK ports into its own emissions trading scheme from July this year, while plans to extend carbon pricing to international voyages from 2028 are also under consideration. The BPA has urged the UK government and the European Commission to reassess the evidence before proceeding with measures that could affect port competitiveness and future investment on both sides of the Channel. articles.body: Americas Europe Tankers International Seaways seals $370m Bruton takeover deal Adis Ajdin October 16, 2026 0 1,593 3 minutes read Bruton Bruton New York-listed tanker owner International Seaways has struck a deal to take over Tor Olav Trøim-backed Bruton in a transaction valuing the Oslo-listed VLCC company at around $370m. The agreement, announced on Friday, will see the Lois Zabrocky-led group acquire Bruton’s entire four-ship supertanker portfolio, going considerably further than the sale of two newbuildings first linked to the US owner in market reports last week. International Seaways has secured agreements with shareholders representing 50.5% of Bruton, including Trøim’s Drew Holdings and Koch Inc, to exchange their holdings for newly issued shares in the US company. The exchange is set at 0.0519 International Seaways shares for each Bruton share, with the initial transaction expected to settle around October 20. The remaining shares will be acquired through a merger, with Seaways expecting to issue approximately 3.12m new shares, accounting for 96% of the total consideration. Smaller Bruton shareholders will receive cash at $6.3044 per share. The deal brings four 300,000 dwt VLCCs into the Seaways fold, including the LNG dual-fuel Mount Vision , which entered service in July, and sistership Mount Horizon , scheduled for delivery from China’s New Times Shipbuilding next month. The remaining two vessels, Mount Frontier and Mount Summit , are due in August and October 2027. The first two ships already have substantial charter cover. Mount Vision secured a 3+1+1-year arrangement with a trading house, earning $95,000 per day for the initial nine months before switching to an index-linked structure. Mount Horizon has been fixed for 12 to 15 months at $105,700 per day. The two 2027 newbuildings remain unchartered and have been at the centre of the recent sale speculation. Splash detailed the potential deal last week after Bruton acknowledged market rumours and launched a strategic review. At the time, International Seaways was linked to the purchase of at least two newbuildings, with brokers discussing values north of $200m per vessel. Bruton’s own figures put the original yard cost of the two 2027 ships at about $117m apiece, highlighting how sharply modern VLCC asset values have moved. The $370m announced on Friday, however, represents the valuation of Bruton’s equity rather than the gross value of its vessels. The takeover follows a major restructuring of Trøim’s tanker interests. Bruton originally built up a 12-ship VLCC programme before splitting the business in August, retaining its first four New Times ships and transferring another eight newbuildings into separately listed OMC Tankers. The demerger left Bruton with a concentrated fleet of near-term deliveries, substantial charter cover and financing arrangements with Chinese lessors covering 85% to 90% of construction costs. The eight vessels in OMC Tankers are not part of the International Seaways transaction. For International Seaways, the acquisition continues an aggressive fleet renewal programme that has seen the company dispose of older tonnage while selectively investing in younger ships. The US owner had a fleet of around 70 vessels, including newbuildings, before the deal. It sold seven older tankers, including two VLCCs, earlier this year for more than $216m and has also invested in LR1 newbuildings at South Korea’s K Shipbuilding. The company strengthened its crude tanker trading platform in January by taking full ownership of Tankers International, which subsequently expanded into the suezmax market. The latest acquisition comes against an exceptionally strong earnings backdrop. Alongside the takeover announcement, International Seaways unveiled preliminary third-quarter net income of $340m to $350m, including a roughly $50m gain from the sale of a suezmax. It reported liquidity of approximately $965m at the end of September. The transaction also brings together businesses associated with two familiar names in Norwegian shipping. Family trusts established by John Fredriksen, Trøim’s former longtime business partner, hold a 13.54% stake in International Seaways, according to the latest US regulatory filing. The pair went their separate ways in 2014 after nearly two decades working together. Bruton’s board has unanimously recommended the transaction, with a shareholder vote expected around October 30. Completion is targeted for early November, subject to the necessary approvals, after which Bruton intends to delist from Euronext Growth Oslo. articles.title: West Africa’s ore boom meets China’s growing VLOC armada
articles.summary: West Africa is fast becoming dry bulk shipping’s biggest growth engine, with its mineral export boom poised to absorb the equivalent of another 120 capesizes by 2030. UK consultancy Tradeviews forecasts in a new report that shipments from the region will surge 50% from 2025 levels to 303m tonnes by the end of the...
articles.body: Africa Dry Cargo West Africa’s ore boom meets China’s growing VLOC armada Sam Chambers October 16, 2026 0 2,321 3 minutes read Winning Winning West Africa is fast becoming dry bulk shipping’s biggest growth engine, with its mineral export boom poised to absorb the equivalent of another 120 capesizes by 2030. UK consultancy Tradeviews forecasts in a new report that shipments from the region will surge 50% from 2025 levels to 303m tonnes by the end of the decade, with Guinea’s giant Simandou iron ore project leading the charge. Crucially for shipowners, the long voyages to China will magnify the impact on vessel demand. “West Africa looks set to remain the fastest growing long-haul source of dry bulk cargo,” Tradeviews stated. The growth is already evident. The five West African exporters covered by the consultancy shipped 160.1m tonnes in their principal trades during the first eight months of this year, up 25% year on year. Liberian iron ore exports nearly doubled to 10.1m tonnes. Tradeviews expects regional exports to reach 267m tonnes next year, with Guinean iron ore shipments climbing to 45m tonnes in 2027 and approximately 112m tonnes by 2030. Bauxite exports, meanwhile, are forecast to retreat from a peak of nearly 194m tonnes this year to 153m tonnes by 2030 as Guinea pushes ahead with domestic alumina processing. A capesize round voyage between Guinea and China takes approximately 78 days, compared with just 29 days on the Australia-China route. Tradeviews calculates that moving a tonne from West Africa consequently absorbs around 2.6 times as much vessel time. On this basis, the consultancy estimates West African trades will require the equivalent of 330 capesizes by 2030, compared with 210 last year. There are, however, already signs that the region’s growth ambitions are running up against freight market realities. In its latest weekly report, BRS Shipbrokers noted that exceptionally high freight rates had priced some higher-cost Guinean bauxite miners out of the export market. Guinea shipped 15.61m tonnes of bauxite in September, down 12% from August, with freight costs at one point accounting for more than half the delivered value of the commodity. The subsequent easing in capesize rates could provide some relief. The C3 benchmark has fallen from $43.43 a tonne in late September to $32.95 on October 12, prompting BRS to suggest Guinean bauxite exports could recover by 5% to 10% month on month during November and December. The broker described the situation as a “test of elasticity” rather than the start of another cargo boom, pointing out that Shandong alumina refineries processing imported ore lost RMB261.8 per tonne in September. SSY has similarly warned that Guinean bauxite exports have retreated from early-September highs, observing that “shipping demand is turning more sensitive to margin levels on the mining side”. Tradeviews did also caution that potential Guinean bauxite export restrictions, Simandou project delays, dedicated ore carriers and the displacement of Australian iron ore shipments could reduce the benefits for the wider capesize market with much of the market increasingly looking like a Chinese conveyor belt. SSY noted in a market report from August that VLOCs of more than 220,000 dwt accounted for nearly half of Simandou shipments during the first half of 2026. More significant for independent owners is what is coming down the slipways. SSY data shows Chinese tonnage accounts for nearly 40% of the current VLOC orderbook, raising questions over how much of Simandou’s enormous prospective tonne-mile demand will ultimately filter through to the conventional capesize spot market. Bauxite’s growing importance to dry bulk shipping will be reflected at next April’s Geneva Dry , the world’s premier commodities shipping conference, with a standalone Bauxite Blitz session. Scheduled for April 28, the discussion will examine the expanding trade, shifting supply patterns and implications for future capesize demand. Confirmed speakers include Ernst Meyer, president and CEO of Torvald Klaveness, and Robert Haggquist, charterer and decarbonisation lead at South32. Braemar’s Derek Langston will moderate the session. articles.title: ScottishPower Renewables completes ‘record-breaking’ cable landfall operation
articles.summary: ScottishPower Renewables has completed what it says was a record-breaking cable landfall operation for its 960 MW East Anglia Two offshore wind...
articles.body: Subsea October 16, 2026 · 2 days ago ScottishPower Renewables completes ‘record-breaking’ cable landfall operation 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email ScottishPower Renewables ScottishPower Renewables has completed what it says was a record-breaking cable landfall operation for its 960 MW East Anglia Two offshore wind farm in the UK, installing two nearly 1.8-kilometer-long ducts beneath the Suffolk coastline and seabed for the project’s export cables. The ducts, each measuring 800 millimeters in diameter, were installed using horizontal directional drilling (HDD), a technique that creates an underground passage without excavating beaches or disturbing the coastline directly. ScottishPower Renewables says the operation involved the world’s longest continuous single sections of extruded polyethylene (PE) ducts and represents the largest electricity transmission landfall of its kind in the UK, based on the combination of duct length and diameter. Manufactured by Pipelife in Norway, the ducts were produced as single uninterrupted lengths, eliminating the need for welded joints. They will provide a protected route for the high-voltage export cables carrying electricity from the offshore wind farm to shore. The landfall works form part of the project’s onshore civil engineering program, led by OCU Group with support from its subsidiary Peter McCormack & Sons. ScottishPower Renewables said the operation also marked a manufacturing record for Pipelife, whose ducts measured approximately 1,793 meters each. “The completion of this colossal HDD, which is three times the length of our other East Anglia projects, is a huge achievement – quite literally – and a major milestone as we progress construction of our third windfarm in the region,” said Ross Ovens , ScottishPower Renewables’ Managing Director for Offshore. “Landfall works are known to be one of the most technically challenging aspects of building an offshore windfarm, but thanks to precision planning and a great partnership with our principal contactor OCU Group and duct manufacturer Pipelife, this programme has well and truly hit the mark – breaking UK and world records in the process.” The milestone comes as East Anglia Two advances towards offshore construction, with the first export cable expected to be installed in summer 2027, and commercial operation targeted for late 2028. The 960 MW offshore wind farm will be built at a site in the southern North Sea, around 33 kilometers off the Suffolk coast at its nearest point, where 64 Siemens Gamesa SG 14-236 DD wind turbines will be installed on monopile foundations. articles.body: Asia Containers HMM commits $1.6bn to 12 more containerships Sam Chambers October 16, 2026 0 1,896 1 minute read HMM HMM South Korea’s HMM is pressing ahead with its fleet expansion programme, approving a $1.62bn investment in 12 containerships comprising eight 13,000 teu newbuildings and four smaller vessels. The Seoul-listed carrier’s board approved spending KRW2.168trn ($1.617bn) yesterday, according to a stock exchange filing. The investment includes fresh orders for eight 13,000 teu ships, alongside the acquisition of three 2,800 teu vessels and one 1,700 teu ship through resale transactions involving newbuildings already under construction. The 12 vessels will add a combined 114,100 teu of capacity, with deliveries scheduled to be completed by December 2029. HMM has yet to identify the shipyards responsible for the eight larger vessels or the sellers of the four smaller ships. Propulsion specifications have also not been disclosed. The latest investment follows last year’s KRW4trn ($2.8bn) commitment covering 12 LNG dual-fuel 13,000 teu containerships and two VLCCs, with HD Hyundai and Hanwha Ocean securing the boxship contracts. Under HMM’s business plan through to 2030, the carrier aims to expand its containership fleet to 166 vessels totalling 1.47m teu by the end of the decade, alongside 110 bulk carriers with a combined capacity of 13.52m dwt.
